messages.subject: Area coverted to 1
messages.body_plain:
A quick question about Area.

 When the area is UNKNOWN and you are converting area to 1 in your analysis,
does your Density Estimate  represent 1 unit of measure (eg: meter or
 meter sq.) or 1 transect?

Thanks,

Pam

messages.subject: Re: Area coverted to 1
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 11 Jan 1999 18:52:35 -0500 (EST), Pamela McRae wrote:

> >
> >A quick question about Area.
> >
> > When the area is UNKNOWN and you are converting area to 1 in your analysis,
> >does your Density Estimate  represent 1 unit of measure (eg: meter or
> > meter sq.) or 1 transect?

Density (D) is always abundance per unit area, whether the area is known or
not.  You will have defined the units of area (e.g., meter sq.) when you set up
the project.

(It is the abundance (N) estimate that is affected by the area that you have
entered in the stratum data layer - if you don't enter anything the default is
1 unit area per stratum.  If you only have one stratum, then total area will be
1 and the density and abundance estimates will be the same (except that
abunance is rounded to the nearest whole number).  Generally though, if your
area is unknown then ignore the abundance estimates.)

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

messages.subject: Distance 3.5 import problem workaround
messages.body_plain:
Summary:

This message is for Distance 3.5 users.  It concerns a problem with the
import data feature.  If you are having problems importing data, read on.  If
not, ignore this message.

Details:

A few users have reported problems using the data import feature in Distance
3.5.  The problem occurs in the Data Import Wizard after pressing the Next
button on the introductory screen, and is manifested by an error message.  In
Release 4 (the latest release), the error message reads: "Couldn't find
installable ISAM. (Error number: 3170)".

If you encounter this problem, use the following work-around.
1. Exit Distance.
2. In Windows, open a DOS command prompt.
3. At the prompt line type:
   regsvr32 c:\windows\system\mstext35.dll  (windows 95 or 98 machines)
   regsvr32 c:\winnt\system32\mstext35.dll  (windows NT machines)
4. Restart Distance.  The problem should have disappeared.
   If not, let me know.

Wishing everyone a happy 1999!

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

messages.body_plain:
I contacted Mark about this problem, and recommended he apply the import
patch I discussed in my Jan 13th post to the distance-sampling list.  This
solved his problem.

FYI, my message to him and his reply are appended below.

 - Len

P.S. Joe Rogen replied:

> >Try given it a shorter name, like 8 characters, hope that helps,

Good suggestion, Joe - many programs have trouble with long file names.
However, D3.5 shouldn't have any problems this - I regularly call my import
files things like "test data import file 25.txt" with no problem.

From: "Distance Development" <dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>
To: "Mark Jacobs" <ma...@trano.freeserve.co.uk>
Date: Mon, 18 Jan 1999 09:53:44
Subject: Re: New problems with data import from EXCEL and SPSS

Hi Mark,

For some reason, your message appeared on the list 3 times.  Did you send it
thrice?

Anyway, hopefully we can save you from the Foreign Legion!

> >I [...] proceed to the data import wizard, choose the file containing the
> >delimited data, and then it all goes horribly wrong I get a message which
> >reads;
> >

> >An error occurred while distance was trying to read the file
> >c:\pfdatamad98
> >please check this file exists and contains delimited data

D3.5 Release 4 includes an error number and error message
after this text, e.g.,
"Couldn't find installable ISAM
(Error number: 3170)"

This message gives us a clue to what's going wrong.  Some of the possible
error numbers are documented in the help file on the page titled "Data Import
Wizard - Troubleshooting", together with possible solutions.

Alternatively, if you're getting the error 3170, the problem is with the
distance setup - I posted a message to the list on Jan 13th about this.  I
notice you joined the list on Jan 16th, so please check the list archives
(http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/archive.html). The 3170
error problem is also documented in the "Known problems in Distance 3.5
Release 4" page, under "Distance Updates and Extras" on the Distance web site
(http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/).

Please email me the error number you're getting, and tell me if any of the
above was any help.  Let's get the problem resoved by private email and then
post a message to the list saying what the solution was.  OK?

 - Len Thomas

Hi Len

Thanks for e-mailing back with regards to my import problem i seem to have
solved it. The problem seems to have been in DISTANCE 3.5 version 3, it
became the solvable problem of error 3170 as soon as i downloaded version 4
off the net. The message that i got in version 3 read:

An error occurred while distance was trying to read the file
c:\pfdatamad98
please check this file exists

So you see there was no number to the error message.  Maybe my computer,
maybe the downloading, maybe a bug in the version 3, who knows but it's all
tickerty boo now cheers.

regards mark

Dear Distance users,

I am experiencing some problems with data file structure.  Below is an
example of how I am attempting to structure my data.

GLOBAL:STUDY SITE	STRATUM: REGION	SAMPLE: POINT COUNT		OBSERVATION:
 LABEL				LABEL		AREA	PLOT NAME	EFFORT	DISTANCE	CLUSTER SIZE
DUMOGA			RAIN FOREST	300,000	1A
DUMOGA			RAIN FOREST	300,000	1B
DUMOGA			RAIN FOREST	300,000	1C
DUMOGA			RAIN FOREST	300,000	1D
DUMOGA			RAIN FOREST	300,000	1E

Qu 1. Is it always necessary to specify an area for the habitat type?

Qu 2. Is effort just the number of times a plot was censused?

My census data was collected from set plots on a weekly basis for a
year.  I would like to be able to obtain weekly/ fortnightly and
monthly densities to correspond with phenological data I also
collected at these times.  My data is therefore also coded by the
month, week and plot, as shown below.

??		??		SAMPLE			OBSERVATION

JAN		1		1A

  				1C

  				1A

Qu 3. What is the data layer/ data layer name for month and week?
Qu 4. What is the effort in this case?  If say a monthly estimate is
asked for can Distance not see how many times the plot was repeated in
the month in order to work the effort out??

I hope someone can assist me with these problems.

Best Regards,

Alexis Cahill (e-mail: a.j.c...@mmu.ac.uk)

messages.subject: Re: problems with data file structuring
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexis,

My answers are given after each question.

On Wed, 20 Jan 1999 11:12:12 GMT, A.J.C...@mmu.ac.uk wrote:

> >Dear Distance users,
> >
> >I am experiencing some problems with data file structure.  Below is an
> >example of how I am attempting to structure my data.
> >
   GLOBAL	      STRATUM           SAMPLE           OBSERVATION
(STUDY SITE)	     (REGION)        (POINT COUNT)           ()
LABEL        LABEL       AREA    PLOT_NAME EFFORT  DISTANCE CLUSTER_SIZE
DUMOGA       RAIN FOREST 300,000 1A
DUMOGA       RAIN FOREST 300,000 1B
DUMOGA	       RAIN FOREST 300,000 1C
DUMOGA       RAIN FOREST 300,000 1D
DUMOGA	       RAIN FOREST 300,000 1E

So, in this example there is one record in the global layer (not surprising,
as distance only allows one record in that layer), one record in the stratum
layer, called Rain Forest, and 5 records in the sample layer, called 1A to
1E.  Right?

> >Qu 1. Is it always necessary to specify an area for the habitat type?

Usually, you will want to input the area of the stratum (habitat type), so
that you can get an estimate of abundance (N) as well as density (D).

However, if you don't know the area of your strata, just leave the area as
the default value (1), and ignore the abundance estimate that comes out of
distance.  In this case you'll only be interested in the density.

For more on this, look at my reply earlier this month to a question "Area
converted to 1", archived on the distance-sampling list web page
(http://www.mailbase.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling/ - Under Message archives,
January 1999).

In the next release of Distance I'm thinking of making the default value of
area 0, in which case no abundance estimate would be made.  Hopefully this
would make things clearer.

> >Qu 2. Is effort just the number of times a plot was censused?

In the case of point counts, usually yes.  For line transects it is line
length.  However, in your case things may be a little more complex (see
below).

(Note - strictly, you should say "surveyed" rather than "censused".  A census
is a complete count.)

> >My census data was collected from set plots on a weekly basis for a
> >year.

I assume you mean that you visited each "plot" (point count location) once a
week each week for a year.  Right?

> > I would like to be able to obtain weekly/ fortnightly and
> >monthly densities to correspond with phenological data I also
> >collected at these times.  My data is therefore also coded by the
> >month, week and plot, as shown below.

  ??   ??       SAMPLE          OBSERVATION
MONTH WEEK   (POINT COUNT)          ()
             LABEL EFFORT  DISTANCE CLUSTER_SIZE
JAN   1     	 1A
         	 1A
              1B
      	        1C
      	        1C
      	        1C
              1D
              1E
      2       1A
              1A

I assume this means that you saw 3 animals (birds?) on point 1A in week 1, 1
animal on point 1B, 3 on point 1C, etc.

> >Qu 3. What is the data layer/ data layer name for month and week?

Related to the next question, so I'll answer both together.

> >Qu 4. What is the effort in this case?  If say a monthly estimate is
> >asked for can Distance not see how many times the plot was repeated in
> >the month in order to work the effort out??

Unfortunately, Distance 3.5 is not set up to deal with repeated survey data.
For that matter the current version is not set up to deal with any more than
one level of stratification either.

There are two ways to deal with this: the straightforward but cumbersome and
the clever but possibly not workable in your case.

Straightforward but cumersome:

This is the way such a problem would have been tackled in previous versions
of Distance.  You'll need to set up 2 projects - one for the monthly analysis
and one for the weekly analysis.

For the monthly analysis, define each month as a stratum (with area 300,000).
Each stratum (month) has 5 samples (points/plots - 1A - 1E).  Each plot is
visited either 4 or 5 times per month (depending on the month), so 4 or 5
will be the effort.  In each plot in each month, pool the observations for
that month and put these in the observation layer.

To get monthly estimates, do a stratified analysis.  You can either estimate
a separate detection function for each stratum (month) or pool the detection
function over months -- perhaps try both and use AIC to tell you which is the
more parsimonious.

If you want an overall estimate for the year, you could either do an
unstratified analysis, or you could combine the stratum estimates to make a
global estimate.  In the latter case, you want to choose the option to take
the mean of the stratum estimates, weighting by the effort in each stratum.

For the weekly analysis, create a second distance project, with each week as
a stratum again with area 300,000.  Each stratum will again have 5 samples
(plots 1A - 1E).  This time the effort is 1 - 1 visit to each plot in each
week.  The observations are the observations on that plot in that week.

To get weekly estimates, do a stratified analysis in this second project.
You probably won't have enough data to estiamte a separate detection funciton
for each week, so you'll likely have to pool.  Unfortunatly, as Distance
doesn't allow multi-level stratification you'll have to pool the deteciton
function right up to year.

Similarly, if you want bi-weekly, create another project file.  If you have
your data in a database or spreadsheet, formatting it for import into these
new project files shouldn't be too big a deal.

Clever but possibly workable in your case:

Alternatively, you could try to do it all in one project, by entering month
and week as extra fields in the observation layer, and then using the post-
stratification feature of distance to post-stratify by week or month.  (Make
sure you've read the User's guide thoroughly before attempting this -
especially the pages on Stratification and post-stratification, and
Multipliers.)

You'd enter your data so it looks like this (in compressed view in the Data
Explorer):

   GLOBAL	STRATUM     SAMPLE        OBSERVATION
(STUDY SITE)	(REGION)    (POINT COUNT) ()
LABEL        LABEL       LABEL         DISTANCE CLUSTER_SIZE MONTH WEEK
DUMOGA       RAIN FOREST 1A            1.43     2            JAN   1
                         1A            2.32     1            JAN   1
                         1A            8.00     1            JAN   1
                         1A            4.32     3            JAN   2
                         1A            3.37     1            JAN   3
                         1A            0.94     2            JAN   4
                         1A            4.04     1            FEB   5
[lines skipped for clarity]
                         1B            12.32    1            JAN   1
                         1B            0.38     1            JAN   2
[lines skipped for clarity]
                         1C            3.02     1            FEB   6
[lines skipped for clarity]
[...]

(Notice that the first entry in plot 1C is for week 6 - implying that no
animals were seen on plot 1C in weeks 1-5 -- just an example.)

Then, to do the weekly analysis you'd post-stratify by Week.  For monthly
analysis, you'd post-stratify by Month.  For the yearly analysis you'd not
stratify at all.

The only hitch here is that you have to manually tell Distance that there is
52 times more effort per sample in the yearly anlaysis than the weekly one.
One way to do this would be to edit the Effort field between analyses -
entering 52 for the yearly analysis and 1 for the weekly one.  However this
is cumbersome, so you can use a trick.  Enter an effort of 1 for each sample.
Then define a multiplier of value 52 and call it something like "Samples per
year".  Now for the yearly analysis, you just need to include this multiplier
in the model definition as a divisor of the density estimate.  For the weekly
analysis no multipier is needed.

Unfortunately, this approach falls down in the monthly analysis.  You could
define a multiplier called "Samples per month", but it would be hard to know
whether to put a value of 4 or 5 in it, as some months have 4 weekly visits
and some 5.  So, I'm not sure this "clever" approach will work for you!

There is one other problem with both approaches to do with the variance
estimation.  Distance doesn't know that plot 1A in month JAN is the same as
plot 1A in month FEB, and treats plots within months (or weeks) as
independent for the purposes of variance estimation.  It isn't using the
information that these are the same plots, and so the variance estimates from
Distance will be over-estimates (I think).  I can't think of a way around
this at present - perhaps someone else on the list can?

If it's any comfort, the next version of Distance (Distance 4, due out in
late 2000) will hopefully include multi-level stratification, repeated
sampling and multipliers at the stratum and sample level, so the analysis
should be rather easier then!

Hope this has helped,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

                     Workshop 1: June 14-17
                     Workshop 2: June 21-24

        Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA

Overview
--------

Distance sampling is the most widely used method for estimating the
abundance of wildlife populations. The aim of these workshops is to
train participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of
distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The two
identical 4-day workshops will be a blend of theory and practice, and
participants will learn the new, windows version of the software Distance.
Participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to
do some preliminary analyses with their data. In the latter part of each
workshop, time is set aside for presentation of more advanced concepts
and discussion of topics of common interest in smaller, informal groups.

messages.subject: Distance 3.5 numerical problem
messages.body_plain:
Summary:

This message is for Distance 3.5 users. It concerns a newly discovered bug in
Distance 3.5 which will likely only affect very few users - those with
stratum areas greater than 1E+07 and some of those using multipliers.  If
this is you, read on.  If not, ignore this message.

We are planning on putting out another release of Distance 3.5 to address
this bug, and some other minor issues, early in February.  Hopefully, we have
now uncovered the important bugs -- we are very much hoping to make Release 5
the last for a while!

 - Len Thomas

Details:

The following is extracted from a new entry on the Known Problems page of
Distance web site (http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/)

Analysis: Problems reading numbers in scientific format (i.e., with
exponents).  This problem manifests itself in two places: (1) areas larger
than 1E+07 are truncated; (2) large or small multipliers are not read in the
analysis engine properly.  You can tell if (1) is a problem in your project
because the area will be displayed in exponent format in the Data Explorer.
For (2), you should check the Multiplier in the first page of the Analysis
Details Results tab is the same as the value in the "Multiplier =" line of
the Log tab.  Workaround: None - this problem will be resolved in a future
release of Distance. [26 Jan 98]

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland
